# Larkspur — Short Brief

## What it is

Larkspur is a **distributed job scheduler for Python**. A scheduler node decides what runs and when; workers pull jobs from a shared **Postgres or Redis** backend and report results back. Key capabilities include:

- **Schedule types:** Cron expressions, fixed intervals, and business-calendar schedules (per-job time zones, misfire handling).
- **Reliability:** Retries with backoff, per-job timeouts, concurrency limits.
- **High availability:** Leader election allows running multiple scheduler nodes.
- **Observability:** Web dashboard for job history and manual runs.

It targets recurring and one-off jobs across a pool of Python workers — a step up from ad-hoc cron hosts.

## License

**Apache License 2.0** — a permissive, commercial-friendly license with an explicit patent grant.

## Who maintains it

- **Project:** Open group of contributors under the "Larkspur project" umbrella.
- **Core team:** Ines Abara (lead), Tomasz Wierzbicki, and Hana Moreau.
- **Sponsorship / commercial support:** **Fennick Labs** sponsors development and offers paid support.
- **Current version:** 2.6.1 (released 30 Aug 2026), with v3.0 development underway.

---

**Bottom line:** Larkspur is an actively developed, Apache-2.0-licensed distributed scheduler for Python with a named core team and corporate backing from Fennick Labs — worth a closer look if you need something more robust than bare cron. ## Python Version Support

Larkspur supports **Python 3.10 through 3.13**. Installation is via `pip`, with optional extras for the Redis backend, Postgres backend, and the web dashboard.

## Cron-Style Schedules

Yes — cron-style scheduling is a first-class feature. Larkspur supports:

- **Standard five-field cron expressions** (minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week), e.g. `30 2 * * 1-5` for 2:30 AM on weekdays.
- **`@` shortcuts:** `@hourly`, `@daily`, `@weekly`, `@monthly`.
- **Per-job time zones** — default is UTC, but you can set any zone (e.g. `tz="Europe/Berlin"`).
- **Misfire handling** — if all scheduler nodes were down when a job was due, you can choose per job whether to skip the missed run or run it once on recovery (`misfire="skip"` or `misfire="run_once"`).

Beyond cron, Larkspur also offers **fixed-interval** schedules (e.g. `every="15m"`) and **business-calendar** schedules that run on business days from a holiday calendar you supply.

## Security Audit & SOC 2 Status

The short answer your security team will want to hear upfront: **no on both counts.**

- **Independent security audit:** Larkspur has **not** had one.
- **SOC 2 report:** Neither the Larkspur project nor Fennick Labs (the sponsoring company) **holds a SOC 2 report.**

The project explicitly acknowledges both gaps on its security page and notes they will update that page if either changes.

## What's in Place Today

That said, Larkspur does have a documented security posture:

- **Vulnerability reporting:** Private disclosure to `security@larkspur-sched.org`, with a 72-hour acknowledgment SLA and a 30-day target for shipping fixes.
- **Supported versions:** The latest minor release (currently 2.6.x) receives security fixes. The prior minor (2.5.x) receives fixes until 31 Dec 2026.
- **Past advisories (2 total):**
  - **LSA-2025-01:** The dashboard's manual-run endpoint didn't require authentication behind certain reverse proxies. Fixed in 2.4.3.
  - **LSA-2026-01:** Job arguments were logged in plain text at `DEBUG` level. Fixed in 2.5.2.

## Takeaway for the Security Team

Larkspur has a reasonable vulnerability disclosure process and a short but clean advisory history, but the absence of both an independent audit and a SOC 2 report is a gap — especially if your organization requires either as a procurement gate. Worth raising directly with Fennick Labs if commercial support is on the table; they may be willing to commission an audit or pursue SOC 2 as a condition of an enterprise contract.

## Single-Scheduler Throughput Ceiling

### Dispatch Rates (per scheduler node)

| Backend | Throughput | Test machine |
|---|---|---|
| **Postgres** | ~5,000 jobs/min | 4 vCPU |
| **Redis** | ~8,000 jobs/min | 4 vCPU |

These are **dispatch rates** — how fast the scheduler can decide what to run and hand jobs to workers. Actual end-to-end throughput depends on the jobs themselves and scales horizontally by adding workers.

### Key Architectural Notes

- **Adding scheduler nodes does not raise the ceiling.** Multiple schedulers exist for *availability*, not throughput. They use leader election through the backend (Postgres advisory locks or Redis), and only the active leader dispatches at any given time.
- **For higher throughput, split into multiple independent Larkspur clusters.** The docs explicitly call this out as the pattern for very large deployments — partition jobs across separate scheduler/backend/worker groups.

### What This Means for You

- At **~5,000–8,000 jobs/min per scheduler**, a single cluster covers most scheduling needs (Tallwater's 1,400-job deployment sits well below this).
- If you ever need to exceed that ceiling, the answer is **multiple independent clusters**, not more scheduler nodes in one cluster.
- Worth noting: the Tallwater case study mentioned advisory-lock contention on a shared Postgres instance during leader changes — so the Postgres backend's real-world ceiling may be lower if it's not on dedicated infrastructure.

# Larkspur — Architecture Brief

## Overview

Larkspur is a distributed job scheduler for Python. A scheduler node decides what runs and when; workers pull jobs from a shared Postgres or Redis backend and report results back. It targets recurring and one-off jobs across a pool of workers — a step up from ad-hoc cron hosts.

**Current version:** 2.6.1 (Aug 2026); v3.0 in development.

## License & Governance

- **License:** Apache 2.0 (permissive, commercial-friendly, explicit patent grant).
- **Core team:** Ines Abara (lead), Tomasz Wierzbicki, Hana Moreau.
- **Sponsor:** Fennick Labs — funds development and offers commercial support.

## Technical Capabilities

|---|---|
| **Python support** | 3.10 – 3.13 |
| **Schedule types** | Five-field cron expressions, `@hourly`/`@daily`/`@weekly`/`@monthly` shortcuts, fixed intervals, business-calendar schedules |
| **Time zones** | Per-job; default UTC |
| **Reliability** | Retries with backoff, per-job timeouts, concurrency limits, misfire handling (skip or run-once) |
| **High availability** | Leader election across multiple scheduler nodes (only the leader dispatches) |
| **Observability** | Web dashboard for job history and manual runs |

## Throughput

- Adding scheduler nodes improves **availability**, not throughput.
- To exceed the single-scheduler ceiling, partition jobs across **multiple independent Larkspur clusters**.
- Worker throughput scales horizontally; add workers as needed.
